# Status report: jf2 allocator test on kestrel, 2026-11-20

**Short version.** jf2 (our fork of the jemalloc memory allocator) lowered the p99 latency (the time within which 99% of requests finish) of kestrel (the key-value store under test) from 2140 us (microseconds) to 870 us, a 59% reduction, on a read-mostly workload. Throughput and median latency stayed inside the run-to-run range. Two items are open: jf2 used 5.7 GB (9.3%) more memory, which needs approval from the capacity team, and the write-heavy workload is not yet tested.

## Words used here

- **kestrel**: the key-value store under test.
- **jemalloc**: the memory allocator library that kestrel uses today, at version 5.3.
- **jf2**: our fork of jemalloc.
- **Build A / Build B**: A is main at commit 4f1c2aa with jemalloc 5.3. B is the same commit with jf2.
- **ycsb-b / ycsb-a**: workloads B and A of YCSB (Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark). B is read-mostly (95% reads, 5% updates). A is write-heavy (50% reads, 50% updates).
- **p50, p99, p99.9**: latency percentiles. p99 is the time within which 99% of requests finish. p50 is the median.
- **Latency spike**: a short period in which latency is much higher than normal.
- **kops/s**: thousand operations per second.
- **RSS**: resident set size, the physical memory that the process holds.
- **Decay purge**: the jemalloc step that returns unused memory to the operating system after a delay.
- **je_arena_decay**: a jemalloc function in the decay purge path.
- **perf**: the Linux profiler.
- **Load average**: the average number of tasks that are running or waiting to run.
- **NUMA pinning**: binding threads and memory to one processor socket (NUMA = non-uniform memory access).
- **logrotate / cron**: logrotate is the system tool that archives log files. cron is the service that starts it every night.
- **Staging**: the pre-production environment.

## Goal

Check whether replacing jemalloc 5.3 with jf2 removes the p99 latency spikes in kestrel.

## Test setup

- **Host**: bench-07, 2 x 32-core Xeon processors (64 cores), 512 GB of memory, Linux kernel 6.8.
- **System load**: the load average was 0.4 before the runs. On 64 cores, this means the host was almost idle.
- **Workload**: ycsb-b with 64 client threads.
- **Runs**: 5 runs per build, 10 minutes per run. The runs alternated A, B, A, B.
- **Reported values**: the median of the 5 runs, with minimum..maximum in parentheses.

## Results

```
Latency in us, median of 5 runs. Scale: 1 character = 250 us.
A = jemalloc 5.3 build, B = jf2 build. Further left is better.

        0       2000    4000    6000    8000    10000
        |-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
p99        B=====A                                 59% lower
           870   2140
p99.9               B==========================A   68% lower
                    3100                       9800
```

Only the p99 and p99.9 latencies changed. Throughput and p50 latency did not change beyond the run-to-run range.

| Metric | A (jemalloc 5.3) | B (jf2) | Change in median |
|---|---|---|---|
| Throughput, kops/s | 412 (405..418) | 409 (401..415) | -3 (-0.7%) |
| p50 latency, us | 118 (116..121) | 119 (117..121) | +1 (+0.8%) |
| p99 latency, us | 2140 (1890..2610) | 870 (820..940) | -1270 (-59%) |
| p99.9 latency, us | 9800 (7200..14100) | 3100 (2700..3900) | -6700 (-68%) |
| RSS at end, GB | 61.2 | 66.9 | +5.7 (+9.3%) |

## What the data shows

- **p99 latency is lower with jf2 in every run.** The highest B run was 940 us. The lowest A run was 1890 us. The two ranges do not overlap.
- **p99.9 latency is lower with jf2 in every run.** The highest B run was 3900 us. The lowest A run was 7200 us.
- **B varies less between runs.** The p99 range of A is 720 us wide (1890..2610). The p99 range of B is 120 us wide (820..940).
- **The test shows no throughput change.** The medians differ by 3 kops/s (0.7%). The ranges overlap (405..418 for A, 401..415 for B).
- **The test shows no p50 latency change.** The medians differ by 1 us (0.8%). The ranges overlap.
- **B uses more memory.** RSS at the end was 5.7 GB (9.3%) higher for B. The notes give one RSS value per build, without a range.

## Cause of the spikes in A

- The spikes in A occurred at the same times as the jemalloc decay purge.
- perf showed that 31% of the samples taken during the spike windows were in je_arena_decay.
- B runs the purge in a background thread.

## One run was replaced

- Run 3 of B stalled for 40 s at minute 7.
- The stall was traced to logrotate, which the nightly cron job started. It was not traced to the allocator.
- The run was repeated. The B results above use the repeat run in place of the stalled run.

## Not tested

- ycsb-a (the write-heavy workload).
- More than 64 client threads.
- NUMA pinning.

The results above apply only to ycsb-b with 64 client threads and no NUMA pinning.

## Open decision

Is the RSS increase of 5.7 GB (9.3%) acceptable? The capacity team must answer.

## Next steps

1. Run ycsb-a tomorrow.
2. Ask the capacity team about the RSS increase.
3. If the capacity team approves, enable jf2 in staging, controlled by a flag (a configuration switch).

---

Notes for you, not part of the report:

- **Workload mixes are my addition.** The 95%/5% and 50%/50% read/update mixes come from the standard YCSB definition, not from your notes. Correct them if kestrel uses a custom mix.
- **Percent changes are computed from the medians.** Your notes gave only the RSS percentage. I calculated the other four.
- **Step 3 gating is ambiguous in the notes.** I wrote it as depending only on the capacity team's approval. Change it if the staging step also waits for the ycsb-a result.
